stories.moot: When a country's leadership changes, its foreign alliances can flip almost overnight — a reminder that geopolitical partnerships are often personal and political, not fixed and permanent.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake death toll rises to 273 as rescuers enter a 'final phase' — but the missing count drops sharply as thousands are found
stories.moot: In the first days after a major disaster, missing-persons counts are usually wildly overstated — communications are down and people are scattered, not necessarily dead. The real toll only comes into focus once search teams can systematically account for everyone.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake toll climbs past 265 as more than 2,700 remain reported missing
stories.moot: Official death tolls after a disaster are almost always undercounts in the first days — the real scale only emerges once rescuers physically reach every blocked-off area and volunteer networks catch missing-persons reports the government hasn't yet verified.

stories.title: Colombia's 72-hour rescue window closes as the toll passes 220 and aid refusals spark backlash
stories.moot: In the first hours after a disaster, a government's choices about accepting outside help can matter as much as the disaster itself — pride or politics in a crisis window can cost lives that logistics alone wouldn't have.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake death toll surges past 220 as new president says 5,000 homes destroyed
stories.moot: In earthquake response, the official death toll almost always rises for days after the initial quake — not because the disaster is worsening, but because rescue teams are still reaching cut-off areas. Early tolls are a floor, not a final count.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake death toll climbs past 160 as rescuers keep digging through rubble
stories.moot: Early death tolls after a disaster are almost always undercounts — the real scale of damage and casualties typically emerges over days as rescue teams reach cut-off areas, which is why responsible reporting keeps updating the number rather than treating the first figure as final.

stories.title: Colombia's new hard-right government recognizes Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights
stories.moot: A country's stance on a decades-old international dispute isn't fixed — it can flip overnight when a new government with a different worldview takes power, which is why elections matter for foreign policy as much as domestic issues.

stories.title: Colombia swears in a hardline right-wing president, ending the Petro era with a promised crackdown on armed groups
stories.moot: When a security-first challenger beats a peace-negotiation incumbent, it's usually because voters judged results, not intentions — persistent violence under a conciliatory approach can open the door for a harder line, regardless of which strategy actually works better long-term.

stories.title: Abelardo de la Espriella sworn in as Colombia's first hard-right president in decades
stories.moot: Elections that follow a period of negotiated peace often swing toward security-first candidates once voters feel violence hasn't actually gone down — peace deals need visible results to survive politically.

west-bengal.name: West Bengal
west-bengal.primer: Tarapith is one of West Bengal's most visited pilgrimage towns, built around a centuries-old Kali temple, and draws heavy footfall during religious observances — the fire broke out on the **third Monday of Shravan**, a Hindu holy month when devotees travel from across the region to perform puja (worship rituals) there. Small pilgrimage-town hotels in India have repeatedly come under scrutiny for weak fire-safety compliance, a recurring issue after past hotel-fire tragedies elsewhere in the country.

stories.title: The Bengal depression is now flooding parts of Odisha, cutting off villages as more rain looms
stories.moot: A weather warning becoming a real flood often isn't about one storm being unusually severe — it's about successive rain systems hitting the same ground before it has time to drain, which is why forecasters watch the gap between systems as closely as the systems themselves.

stories.title: A hotel fire kills at least 7 Shravan pilgrims in West Bengal's Tarapith; the owner is arrested as claims of a blocked exit emerge
stories.moot: Fire-safety rules only protect people if they're actually enforced day-to-day, not just written down — a locked emergency exit turns a manageable fire into a fatal one, regardless of what regulations say on paper.

stories.title: A TMC-linked panchayat chief is among 3 arrested in the killing of a Bengal Congress leader and his son
stories.moot: In India's local politics, the smallest elected offices — village panchayats — often carry the highest stakes for patronage and control, which is why panchayat-level rivalries can escalate to violence more readily than higher, more visible levels of politics.

stories.title: IMD issues red alert as fresh Bay of Bengal low-pressure system threatens Odisha, Bengal and Jharkhand with extreme rain
stories.moot: Monsoon risk doesn't spread evenly across a season — a handful of fast-forming low-pressure systems can concentrate a huge share of a region's flood damage into just a few days, which is why early warnings matter more than seasonal totals.

stories.title: West Bengal Congress holds statewide 'black day' after Nadia double killing
stories.moot: In places with a long history of political violence, an unsolved killing doesn't stay a local crime story for long — it quickly becomes a test of the ruling party's credibility, because how fast (or slowly) police act is read as a signal about whose safety the state actually protects.

stories.title: West Bengal Congress leader and his son shot dead in Nadia, ahead of state elections
stories.moot: In states with a long history of political violence, a single local killing can carry outsized weight — it's read less as an isolated crime and more as a signal about how safe it is to be a political worker on the losing side, right as an election approaches.

stories.title: IPL wicketkeeper Abhishek Porel arrested in rape and blackmail case
stories.moot: A sports league's commercial value doesn't shield contracted athletes from ordinary legal accountability — franchises increasingly have to navigate reputational and contractual questions when a player faces serious criminal allegations.

stories.title: Mamata Banerjee's convoy pelted with mud and stones in Halisahar as TMC's post-defeat anger boils over
stories.moot: Losing power can be more politically dangerous than holding it: once a leader's protective machinery is gone, unresolved local grievances that were suppressed for years can surface suddenly and personally.

indiana.name: Indiana
indiana.primer: Indiana and neighboring Ohio were hit by days of extreme rainfall in mid-August 2026 — far beyond what the region's rivers and drainage systems are built to handle. The White River runs through Indianapolis, the state capital, and had held a flood-height record since **1913** — a record that, notably, included meltwater from snow, unlike this year's flood, which was driven by rain alone. Extreme, fast-moving rainstorms like this are consistent with a broader trend scientists link to a warming atmosphere, which can hold and dump more moisture at once.

stories.title: Indiana's White River shatters a 113-year-old flood record; at least 7 dead as Trump approves federal disaster aid
stories.moot: Infrastructure and flood records built around historical rainfall patterns can be overwhelmed when extreme weather events exceed what engineers originally planned for — a 'once in a century' benchmark isn't a ceiling, it's just the worst case anyone had seen yet.

stories.title: Relentless storms flood the US Midwest; Indiana declares disaster and asks for federal help
stories.moot: Flood damage isn't just about how much rain falls — it's about how saturated the ground already is. The same storm that's a non-event on dry soil can be catastrophic when it lands on ground still soaked from the last one, which is why back-to-back storm systems are so much more dangerous than isolated ones.

stories.title: A derecho and flash floods kill at least two and cut power to 800,000 across the US Midwest
stories.moot: A single storm system can combine tornado-strength winds with flash-flood rainfall, which is why a 'severe thunderstorm' warning can sometimes be as dangerous as a tornado warning — the total damage footprint of a derecho is often far larger.

asia-pacific.name: Asia-Pacific
asia-pacific.primer: The US Navy normally rotates aircraft carriers so no single ship or crew stays deployed indefinitely — carriers need maintenance, and sailors need to go home. The **USS Abraham Lincoln** was sent to the Middle East to support US operations against Iran and has stayed far longer than planned as the conflict dragged on, becoming one of the longest carrier deployments in modern US Navy history. The USS George Washington was the Navy's only carrier permanently based in Asia (forward-deployed to Japan), making it the closest available replacement even though pulling it out weakens America's naval presence facing China.

stories.title: The US is pulling its only forward-deployed Pacific carrier to relieve a crisis-hit USS Lincoln in the Middle East
stories.moot: Militaries — like any system running at capacity — break down in predictable, human ways when a mission runs longer than planned and there's no reserve to rotate in. Overstretch shows up first not in headlines, but in maintenance backlogs and crew welfare.

stories.title: The US pulls its last aircraft carrier out of the Pacific, as the Iran war strains the Navy and leaves China's backyard uncovered
stories.moot: A military can only be in so many places with a fixed number of high-end assets — committing more forces to one crisis always means less coverage somewhere else, even for a superpower.

stories.title: The US Navy sends a new aircraft carrier to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln after sailors tried to jump ship
stories.moot: Militaries generally can't sustain 'maximum pressure' forever with a single unit — extended deployments strain people and equipment, which is why sustained standoffs usually require a rotation plan, not just an initial show of force.
